# vibeward — full reference for LLMs

> Read-only scanner and guardrail for AI-generated / vibe-coded apps and websites. One command
> returns two verdicts that never share a scale: security (exposed secrets, missing Row-Level
> Security, Firebase exposure, insecure backends) and website quality / AI visibility (missing
> metadata, sitemap, structured data, llms.txt, AI crawlers turned away). Deterministic — no LLM
> call. Open source (MIT). Current version 0.3.0. Run with `npx vibeward@latest`.
> Site: https://vibeward.ai

## Why it exists

Things built with AI coding tools (Lovable, Bolt, v0, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex) ship fast and
ship the same handful of holes. Apps leak API keys, forget Row-Level Security and check
authorization in the browser. Websites ship with no metadata, no sitemap and a robots.txt that
blocks the AI assistants people now search with — invisible to Google and to ChatGPT alike.

This is documented, not hypothetical:

- CVE-2025-48757 (CVSS 9.3): insufficient Supabase Row-Level Security in Lovable let
  unauthenticated attackers read/write arbitrary tables. 170 of 1,645 analyzed projects
  (10.3%) were vulnerable.
- Moltbook (2026): a vibe-coded app with no RLS policies and a public key in the client bundle
  exposed ~1.5M auth tokens and 35,000 emails.
- Veracode (2025): AI-generated code introduced a known security flaw in 45% of tests.

## The core design rule: two scales, never mixed

A missing favicon must never share a scale with an exposed service key. So:

- Security findings are counted by severity, written to the SARIF file, and set exit code 2 when
  a critical is present. No config file can silence them.
- Website findings live in their own report section with their own scale. They are excluded from
  the severity counts, from SARIF and from the exit code. `--no-web` skips the pass entirely.

## What it scans — security

Secrets (URL bundles and source code, reported with file:line):
- Supabase service_role key in the client, decoded from the JWT role so the public anon key is
  not falsely flagged, plus the new-format `sb_secret_` key
- Stripe, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, AWS, GitHub, Slack, Resend, SendGrid, Twilio keys
- Database connection strings, private PEM keys and suspicious secret assignments
- Committed .env files

Supabase / Postgres:
- Enumerates the exposed tables live from the data API (falling back to common names), then
  probes each with the public key — including new-format `sb_publishable_` keys. If a table
  returns data, RLS is broken.
- Flags which columns hold personal data, scans returned rows for leaked third-party secrets,
  and checks GraphQL introspection
- `--write-test` adds an opt-in, non-mutating check for unauthenticated writes (an empty insert)
- Migrations: tables created without RLS, permissive `USING (true)` policies, SECURITY DEFINER
  functions
- Optional deep audit via a read-only SQL query you run yourself in the Supabase SQL Editor (no
  credentials shared with the tool)

Firebase:
- Detects the client config and probes for an open Realtime Database and a publicly listable
  Storage bucket

Server-rendered stacks (Next.js with Prisma or Drizzle):
- Missing security headers in next.config
- Server actions and route handlers that mutate data with no auth guard
- Formula injection in Excel/CSV exports

Backend:
- SQL injection (interpolated queries, Prisma $queryRawUnsafe, Drizzle sql.raw, better-sqlite3)
- Open CORS, command injection, eval / new Function, verbose error leaks

Source and local database:
- Exposed .map source maps shipped in the build
- Committed SQLite / .db files, including files served from a public folder

HTTP security headers:
- Missing Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options; technology-stack leaks

Not claimed: the deeper server-side classes (IDOR/BOLA behind a login, rate limiting, orphaned
datastores, business logic) are the manual part of an audit, not something an automated scan
should assert.

## What it scans — website quality and AI visibility (new in 0.3.0)

Every URL scan also crawls up to 8 same-host pages and reports:

AI visibility:
- robots.txt blocking GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, CCBot, Google-Extended and others
- Missing llms.txt

Search and social:
- Missing <title>, or the same <title> on every page
- Missing meta description, canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD structured data, sitemap.xml

Structure and accessibility:
- Zero or multiple <h1> per page
- Missing lang attribute on <html>
- Images with no alt text

Quality:
- No real 404 for unknown URLs
- Missing favicon
- Broken assets (a 404 on a <script> or <img> is also a console error)
- JavaScript console errors on load — needs a real browser, so Playwright is used if it happens
  to be installed; if not, the scan says so and falls back to what it can prove without one
- Uncompressed JS bundle over 1 MB

Vibe-coded fingerprint, scored out of 12:
- Still on a platform domain (*.vercel.app, *.netlify.app, *.lovable.app, *.pages.dev, ...)
- Detected framework
- Empty view-source (an HTML shell with no real content)

This is not Lighthouse. vibeward detects binary absences — the tag is not there, the file was
never generated — which is exactly what a vibe-coded site is missing. Core Web Vitals and full
WCAG auditing are deliberately out of scope.

## vibeward.json — declaring what the site is meant to be

Some "problems" are decisions. Drop a vibeward.json next to the project (or point at one with
`--config`):

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "intent": { "aiCrawlers": "blocked", "siteType": "website" },
  "suppress": [{ "id": "web_missing_og", "reason": "private landing, never shared" }]
}
```

`intent` is not a mute button. Declaring `aiCrawlers: "blocked"` stops vibeward calling that a
mistake — and turns the question around: are you blocked as thoroughly as you think? If the
robots.txt shuts out three of the twelve AI crawlers, that incomplete block becomes the finding.

`siteType` switches off a whole family in one line: an `internal` tool is not judged on sitemaps,
Open Graph or canonical URLs, but still on broken assets and alt text.

`suppress` never hides anything. Every entry needs a reason, the report prints "produced with N
suppression(s) in effect" under the verdict and lists each declared reason. Only website checks
can be suppressed — a security finding cannot be silenced by a config file, by design.

The file is read from local disk only, never fetched from the site being scanned: otherwise
anyone could silence their own audit by uploading a file to their own server.

## Guardrail — stopping the request before the code exists

Most vibe-coded holes start with a prompt. vibeward runs as a Claude Code `UserPromptSubmit` hook
and catches the risky request the moment the user types it — before the agent acts:
- "disable RLS so it works" → blocked, with why + the safe policy to write instead
- "use the service_role key in the frontend" → blocked
- "make the table public to debug" / "remove the login for now" → blocked

The rules are deterministic (no LLM call), so they cannot be prompt-injected away. Install:
```json
{ "hooks": { "UserPromptSubmit": [ { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "npx vibeward@latest guard" }] } ] } }
```
Use `guard --warn` to warn without blocking.

## vibeward init — installing into your AI tools

```
npx vibeward@latest init
```

An interactive picker asks where (this project or your user account) and what, pre-checking
whatever it detects in the repo: a Claude Code skill (audit + fix), the Claude Code guard hook, a
Cursor rule, AGENTS.md, a Windsurf/Devin rule, and a GitHub Action workflow. Options the chosen
scope cannot take are shown greyed out with the reason rather than hidden.

It previews every file before touching disk, never overwrites a file it did not write, merges
settings.json key by key and AGENTS.md between markers — so re-running is how you update. It backs
up any existing file to `<file>.vibeward.bak` before its first change. Non-interactive:

```
vibeward init --scope project --targets claude-skill,claude-hook,cursor --yes
vibeward init --scope user --all --yes
```

Why a skill: the deterministic package detects, the agent fixes. An agent asked "is the meta
description missing?" hallucinates; a parser answering yes/no never does. So vibeward reports, the
skill applies the fixes it can, and then re-runs vibeward to verify — detect, fix, re-detect, the
same loop as a test suite. Every finding carries a `fix` and an `autofix` field (auto /
needs-input / manual) telling the agent exactly how far it may go on its own.

The installed instructions are explicit that security findings are never auto-fixed: deleting an
exposed key from a bundle does not un-leak it, and only the owner decides when it is rotated and
whether the incident must be disclosed.

Note: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md. If you install only the AGENTS.md target, add
`@AGENTS.md` as the first line of your CLAUDE.md — or install the Claude Code skill, which init
offers first.

## Modes

Black-box (from a URL) — quick outside-in check:
```
npx vibeward@latest https://your-app.lovable.app
npx vibeward@latest https://your-app.lovable.app --passive   # public assets only, no data probing
```

White-box (from the code) — deep audit with exact file:line; reads a git repo, a downloaded ZIP
from v0/Bolt/Lovable, or a synced folder:
```
npx vibeward@latest scan ./your-app
```

Supabase deep audit without giving credentials:
```
npx vibeward@latest supabase-sql          # run this query in the Supabase SQL Editor
npx vibeward@latest scan ./your-app --supabase result.json
```

Agents and CI — JSON payload on stdout, every human-facing line on stderr, so it pipes straight
into a parser. No colors, no prompts, no report files unless you pass `--out`. The payload carries
a schemaVersion:
```
npx vibeward@latest https://your-app.com --json --stdout --yes
```

GitHub Action — runs on every push, uploads SARIF to the GitHub Security tab, fails the build on a
critical finding. Takes a folder (`path`) or a deployed URL (`url`):
```yaml
- uses: JSiapoDEV/vibeward@v0.3.0
  with:
    url: https://your-app.com
```

## Flags

- `--passive` — URL mode: read only public assets (bundles, headers, pages), no data probing
- `--write-test` — URL mode: opt-in, non-mutating check for unauthenticated writes
- `--no-web` — URL mode: skip the website quality / AI-visibility checks
- `--config <file>` — path to a vibeward.json (default: beside the target, then the cwd)
- `--supabase <file.json>` — fold in a Supabase audit export
- `--supabase-url <url>` / `--anon-key <key>` — Supabase config if not auto-detected
- `--no-rls` — skip the Row-Level Security probe
- `--sarif <file>` — write SARIF 2.1.0 for GitHub code scanning (security findings only)
- `--out <file.md>` — report path
- `--json` — also dump raw findings as JSON
- `--stdout` — JSON payload on stdout, everything else on stderr (implies --yes)
- `--yes` — confirm authorization without the interactive prompt

## Output

Every finding is a context block designed to be both human-readable and consumable by an AI coding
assistant to open a correct pull request. Each finding includes:
- Classification (CWE)
- Where (URL, bundle, or file:line)
- Evidence (counts, snippets, column names)
- How it's exploited (a concrete abuse path for that instance)
- Impact (quantified: rows, data, money at risk)
- Why it matters (in business language)
- A `fix`, and an `autofix` level: auto, needs-input, or manual
- References (CVE, CWE, vendor docs)

Reports are written as Markdown; JSON and SARIF 2.1.0 are also available. Exit code is 2 when a
critical security finding is present. Website findings never change the exit code.

## Authorization

Scanning is strictly read-only: no writes, no deletes, no data exfiltration. It only reads what a
browser would fetch, and confirms database exposure by reading at most one row (storing only the
count and the names of sensitive columns, never row contents). `--write-test` is the single
opt-in exception and must only be used with explicit authorization.

`vibeward init` is the one command that writes, and only into your own project, after showing you
exactly which files it will touch.

Run it only against applications whose owner hired or authorized you to audit them. Scanning
systems you do not own without permission may be illegal.
